# Neanderthal ancestry trajectory

In this case study, you will be reproducing an important result from [my 2018
study](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1814338116) on the limits of
selection against Neanderthal introgression. In a very unplanned and
unpredictable manner, this research ended up turning into a study on the
importance of model assumptions on the robustness of inferences with $f_4$
statistics and how they can produce entirely misleading inferences about ancient
admixture events in human history.

I chose this case study for several reasons:

1. This research would've been absolutely impossible without simulations exactly
like those you've learned to do in this workshop.

2. The limitations of computational tools I had available at the time required
me to write hundreds of lines of code spread across shell scripts, Python
scripts, and R scripts. Thanks to _slendr_, a project which required months of
work and lots of coding is possible to do in a handful of lines of R.

3. It provides an excellent educational example of how _slendr_ simulations can
help you navigate practically any demographic scenario, gain confidence in your
results, and aid in their interpretation.

4. **Most importantly, the lessons of my paper apply in any context of using
$f_4$ statistics in ancient DNA research. The Neanderthal introgression case
serves just as an illustrative example.**

---

## Preparation

**To avoid too much frustration with transcribing very complex admixture graph
model from yet another of my drawings, please copy the following code into a new
script `introgression.R`. When you visualize the model, you should see a
relatively detailed (yet still simplified) model of ancient human history
including Neanderthal introgression into the ancestors of non-Africans. Again,
please inspect this script to make sure you understand what it does---this is
now even more important than before.**

Please note that real-world simulations are rather computationally intensive,
much more so than the modeling we did in our exercises. Generally speaking, most
of simulation-based research happens on big computational servers. For our
learning purposes here, if things take too long, just lower the amount of
simulated sequence. However, be aware that this will, in turn, make statistics
much more noisy (but that's OK, we're learning here).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the the script `introgression.R`

```{r}
#| outputs: false
#| eval: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

outgroup <- population("outgroup",   time = 7000000, N = 10000)

ancestor <- population("ancestor",   time = 6000001, N =  1000, parent = outgroup, remove = 599999)

altai    <- population("Altai",      time =  600000, N =  1000, parent = ancestor, remove = 49999)
vindija  <- population("Vindija",    time =  200000, N =  1000, parent = altai, remove = 49999)

san      <- population("San",        time =  600000, N = 10000, parent = ancestor)
mbuti    <- population("Mbuti",      time =  350000, N = 10000, parent = san)
yoruba   <- population("Yoruba",     time =  220000, N = 10000, parent = mbuti)
dinka    <- population("Dinka",      time =  150000, N = 15000, parent = yoruba)

nonafr   <- population("nonAfrican", time =   70000, N = 3000,  parent = dinka)

gf <- gene_flow(from = vindija, to = nonafr, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, ancestor, altai, vindija, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 30
)

# schedule recording of present-day individuals
schedule_present <- schedule_recording(
  model, times = 0,
  list(outgroup, 1), list(san, 1), list(mbuti, 1), list(yoruba, 1), list(dinka, 1), list(nonafr, 1)
)

# schedule recording of two Nenderthals
schedule_neand <- schedule_recording(model, times = 50000, list(altai, 1, "Altai"), list(vindija, 1, "Vindija"))

# schedule recording of Upper-Paleolithic modern humans
schedule_emh <- schedule_recording(model, times = runif(n = 50, min = 1000, max = 45000), list(nonafr, 1))

# bind the schedules into one
schedule <- rbind(schedule_present, schedule_neand, schedule_emh)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

Here's the model visualization (very janky, I know, but it is what it is...):

## Indirect $f_4$-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry

The main controversy at the time I did this research was caused by the
observation that ancient DNA time series of early modern humans (like the one
you just simulated!) showed [a clear
decline](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17993/figures/2) in Neanderthal
ancestry trajectory over the past ~45 thousand years.

The way the authors of the "Neanderthal decline" paper computed Neanderthal
ancestry was using what I ended up naming as the "indirect $f_4$-ratio"
estimate, described in panel B of [Figure
1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1814338116#fig01) in my paper (where
"Dinka" typically represented the "East African" lineage, and "Yoruba"
represented the "Central and West African" lineage, to follow the terminology in
that schematic diagram). This "indirect" estimate is what showed clear evidence
of the decline in Neanderthal ancestry over time.

---

**Compute this "indirect $f_4$-ratio" estimate of Neanderthal ancestry from your
simulated `ts` tree sequence for every one of your "nonAfrican" individuals.
Then visualize the simulated Neanderthal ancestry trajectory as a time-series
(i.e., your indirect ancestry estimate on the y-axis, time on the x-axis),
similarly to what's shown for the empirical data linked above. What kind of
temporal trend do you observe?**

**Hint:** You can either compute this "manually" using the path overlap
principles described in the $f$ statistics chapter earlier, or you can make your
life a bit easier and use a dedicated _slendr_ function `ts_f4ratio()`. That
function follows the same nomenclature shown in my [Figure
1B](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1814338116#fig01) diagram above. If
you use `ts_f4ratio()`, be aware that `X` can only always be one individual in
this function, so you will want to compute this for every aDNA individual in the
time-series separately.

**Hint:** If you need more help, see this example of how to compute the indirect
$f_4$-ratio for a single individual.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the hint

Here's a manual calculation of the "indirect $f_4$-ratio" as a ratio of two
$f_4$ statistics for a single individual "nonAfrican_1":

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["Yoruba"], X = s["outgroup"], Y = "nonAfrican_1", Z = "Vindija")$f4 /
ts_f4(ts, W = s["Yoruba"], X = s["outgroup"], Y = s["Dinka"], Z = "Vindija")$f4
```

Here's how the function `ts_f4ratio()` can be used for the same purpose:

```{r}
ts_f4ratio(ts, X = "nonAfrican_1", A = s["Yoruba"], B = s["Dinka"], C = "Altai", O = s["outgroup"])
```

Note, however, that this estimate effectively infers the "modern human ancestry"
represented by our shared genetic roots in Africa. To arrive to a Neanderthal
ancestry estimate, we need to compute it's complement:

```{r}
1 - ts_f4ratio(ts, X = "nonAfrican_1", A = s["Yoruba"], B = s["Dinka"], C = "Altai", O = s["outgroup"])$alpha
```

This is close to our simulated 3% Neanderthal ancestry proportion, which is
reassuring!

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's what my simulated trajectory looks like:

```{r}
#| echo: false
rm(ts)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# sss <- as.integer(runif(n = 10, min = 1, max = 999999))
#                   
# for (seed in sss) {
#   cat(seed, "\n")
  # pdf(paste0("files/introgression/indirect_base_", seed, ".pdf"))
# ts <-
#   msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule, random_seed = seed) %>%
#   ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = seed)

if (!file.exists("files/introgression/base_indirect.rds")) {
indirect_base <-
  ts_recorded(ts) %>%                 # get the table of individuals
  filter(pop == "nonAfrican") %>%     # filter it down to only non-Africans
  mutate(
    ancestry =                        # compute the "indirect" estimate for each individual
      sapply(name, function(x) {
        1 - ts_f4ratio(ts, X = x, A = s["Yoruba"], B = s["Dinka"], C = "Altai", O = s["outgroup"])$alpha
      })
  )

p <- ggplot(indirect_base, aes(time, ancestry)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlim(45000, 0) +
  ylim(0, 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ggtitle("Indirect f4-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry over time") +
  xlab("time before present") +
  ylab("Neanderthal ancestry proportion")
  saveRDS(p, "files/introgression/base_indirect.rds")
} else {
  p <- readRDS("files/introgression/base_indirect.rds")
}
p
```

## Adding complex admixture during modern human prehistory

In your visualization of the indirect $f_4$-ratio trajectory, you should have
noticed no trend at all. Indeed, under neutrality, Neanderthal ancestry is
expected to constant throughout the millenia. However, the puzzle at the time
was that the empirical data showed clear, significant temporal decline in this
estimate over time!

The solution to the puzzle came out of (lots of) simulations and modeling, very
similar to what you've done in this workshop so far. Let's retrace my steps
again.

---

**What happens if you introduce additional gene flow events _within_ the modern
human population tree? For example, simulate admixture between the two African
lineages used in your indirect $f_4$-ratio calculation, as well as "back-flow"
admixture from the non-African population into both of those African lineages.
Let's say that all of these admixture events should happen at 5% proportion, the
within-Africa gene flow should happen starting from 20 kya until present-day
time 0, and the backflow nonAfrican admixture should happen from 8 kya to 5
kya.**

None of those changes into the demographic model changes the amount of true
Neanderthal ancestry in Europeans. But **what does the trajectory of the
indirect Neanderthal ancestry estimate look like when you compute it on this
model with additional complex admixture within modern humans?**

**Hint:** Feel free to make a copy of your `introgression.R` script to make the
indicated changes, perhaps saving it as `introgression_complex.R`, just to make
things clean and tidy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's what my simulated trajectory looks like on the modified model:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

gf <- list(
  # Neanderthal introgression
  gene_flow(from = vindija, to = nonafr, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000),
  # admixture within Africa
  gene_flow(from = yoruba, to = dinka, proportion = 0.05, start = 20000, end = 0),
  gene_flow(from = dinka, to = yoruba, proportion = 0.05, start = 20000, end = 0),
  # "backflow" admixture from Eurasia to Africa
  gene_flow(from = nonafr, to = dinka, proportion = 0.05, start = 8000, end = 5000),
  gene_flow(from = nonafr, to = yoruba, proportion = 0.05, start = 8000, end = 5000)
)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, ancestor, altai, vindija, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 30
)

# sss <- as.integer(runif(n = 20, min = 1, max = 999999))

# for (seed in sss) {
#   cat(seed, "\n")
# ts <-
#   msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule, random_seed = seed) %>%
#   ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = seed)

ts <- ts_read("files/introgression/admix_725458.trees", model = model)
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

indirect_admix <-
  ts_recorded(ts) %>%                 # get the table of individuals
  filter(pop == "nonAfrican") %>%     # filter it down to only non-Africans
  mutate(
    ancestry =                        # compute the "indirect" estimate for each individual
      sapply(name, function(x) {
        1 - ts_f4ratio(ts, X = x, A = s["Yoruba"], B = s["Dinka"], C = "Altai", O = s["outgroup"])$alpha
      })
  )

direct_admix <-
  ts_recorded(ts) %>%                 # get the table of individuals
  filter(pop == "nonAfrican") %>%     # filter it down to only non-Africans
  mutate(
    ancestry =                        # compute the "indirect" estimate for each individual
      sapply(name, function(x) {
        ts_f4ratio(ts, X = x, A = "Altai", B = "Vindija", C = s["Dinka"], O = s["outgroup"])$alpha
      })
  )

if (!file.exists("files/introgression/admix_indirect.rds")) {
p1 <- ggplot(indirect_admix, aes(time, ancestry)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlim(45000, 0) +
  ylim(0, 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ggtitle("Indirect f4-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry over time") +
  xlab("time before present") +
  ylab("Neanderthal ancestry proportion")
  saveRDS(p1, "files/introgression/admix_indirect.rds")
} else {
  p1 <- readRDS("files/introgression/admix_indirect.rds")
}

if (!file.exists("files/introgression/admix_direct.rds")) {
p2 <- ggplot(direct_admix, aes(time, ancestry)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlim(45000, 0) +
  ylim(0, 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ggtitle("Direct f4-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry over time") +
  xlab("time before present") +
  ylab("Neanderthal ancestry proportion")
  saveRDS(p2, "files/introgression/admix_direct.rds")
} else {
  p2 <- readRDS("files/introgression/admix_direct.rds")
}
p1

  # ts_save(ts, paste0("files/introgression/admix_", seed, ".trees"))
# }
```

We pick up a decline in Neanderthal ancestry even though we know there's no
decline at all! This is because the indirect $f_4$-ratio make very strong
assumptions about the population tree of modern humans, specifically the fact
that there was no admixture between different modern human lineages after
Neanderthal introgression.

Don't worry if your own result is noisy! That's what replicate simulations are
for (remember the existence of the `ts_replicate()` function, which I wrote
exactly for this purpose).

:::








## Direct $f_4$-ratio estimate of Neanderthal ancestry

The reason we had to compute Neanderthal ancestry using the "indirect" statistic
is because we only had a single Neanderthal genome available at the time---the
genome of the "Altai" Neanderthal.

Luckily, a few years later, a second Neanderthal was sequenced which allowed us
to express the $f_4$-ratio estimate in a "direct" way using both Neanderthal
genomes. We called this estimate the "direct $f_4$-ratio" estimate.

If you got to the [relevant part of the $f$-statistics
chapter](https://bodkan.net/simgen/tree-thinking.html#exercise-estimating-admixture-proportions),
you may remember that we discovered multiple ways of computing the `px`
ancestry---either coming from the `p3` population (we could call it `alpha`), or
as its complement coming from the `p2` population (we could compute it as `1 -
alpha`). Well, the "indirect vs direct $f_4$-ratio" situation is exactly the
same.

**Using this idea, compute the "direct $f_4$-ratio" using the two Neanderthal
genomes on the model which includes lots of complex admixture within modern
humans. How does the direct $f_4$-ratio perform on such a model? Is it robust
and can it infer the Neanderthal ancestry trajectory accurately, unlike the
indirect estimate?**


**Hint:** If you need help, see this example of how to compute the direct
$f_4$-ratio for a single individual again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the hint

Here's how the function `ts_f4ratio()` can be used for this calculation.
Basically, we exchange the two African lineages for the two Neanderthal
lineages, it's as simple as that:

```{r}
ts_f4ratio(ts, X = "nonAfrican_1", A = "Altai", B = "Vindija", C = s["Dinka"], O = s["outgroup"])
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's what my simulated trajectory looks like on the modified model:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
p2
```

Don't worry if your own result is noisy! That's what replicate simulations are
for (remember the existence of the `ts_replicate()` function, which I wrote
exactly for this purpose).

Finally, here's a comparison of both indirect and direct $f_4$-ratio statistics
against one another. Again, bear in mind that in reality (which we know from the
simulations) the proportion of Neanderthal ancestry remained the same over tens
of thousands of years---but the indirect $f_4$-ratio statistic gives us a
misleading result, because it makes assumptions about modern human population
relationships which simply do not hold:

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (!file.exists("files/introgression/admix_comparison.rds")) {
p <- rbind(
  indirect_admix %>% mutate(estimate = "indirect f4-ratio"),
  direct_admix %>% mutate(estimate = "direct f4-ratio")
) %>% 
ggplot(aes(time, ancestry, color = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlim(45000, 0) +
  ylim(0, 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ggtitle("Indirect vs direct f4-ratio estimates") +
  xlab("time before present") +
  ylab("Neanderthal ancestry proportion")
  saveRDS(p, "files/introgression/admix_comparison.rds")
} else {
  p <- readRDS("files/introgression/admix_comparison.rds")
}
p
```


:::

---

**In conclusion, the demographic simulation exploration in [my
paper](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1814338116) took months of work
(and a combination of Python simulations, shells scripts, and R data analysis
scripts), resolving a problem which occupied the brightest minds of population
genetics at the time. I hope that the fact that you're able to reproduce the
core aspects of this work this easily convinces you of the power of _slendr_
modeling for this type of research!**









## Bonus exercise

Because I saved you a lot of work by providing the introgression admixture model
already programmed, here's a bonus challenge:

One question that the authors of the [original draft Neanderthal genome
paper](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1188021) had to answer was
the issue of the direction of gene-flow.

**How would you show that introgression happened from Neanderthals into
non-Africans and not the other way around? Skim through the paper linked above,
particularly focusing on the section called _"Direction of gene flow"_ to get an
idea of how did the authors distinguished the two scenarios using a $D$
statistic (which, for our purposes, could be thought of as essentially
equivalent to the $f_4$ statistic as we've established it, so you can use the
familiar $f_4$ to answer this question).**

**Hint:** They used logic to argue for what would the expected values of certain
$f_4$ statistics look like between two different models (the model of
introgression from Neanderthals into non-Africans, and the model of
introgression from non-Africans into Neanderthals). We want to use simulations
to try to arrive at the same conclusions.


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false

#
#
# This is unfinished and likely non-working sketch of the original code.
#
#

model2 <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, altai, vindija, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gene_flow(from = nonafr, to = vindija, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000),
  generation_time = 30
)
schedule2 <- schedule_recording(model2, times = 0, list("each", 5))

plot_grid(
  plot_model(model1, proportions = TRUE, log = TRUE),
  plot_model(model2, proportions = TRUE, log = TRUE)
)

result1 <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10,
  {
    ts1 <- msprime(model1, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule1) %>% ts_mutate(1e-8)

    samples <- ts_names(ts1, split = TRUE)

    bind_rows(
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["San"],    X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["Mbuti"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["Yoruba"], X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["Dinka"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"])
    )
  }
) %>% mutate(direction = "Nea -> MH")

result2 <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10,
  {
    ts2 <- msprime(model2, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule1) %>% ts_mutate(1e-8)

    samples <- ts_names(ts2, split = TRUE)

    bind_rows(
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["San"],    X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Mbuti"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Yoruba"], X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Dinka"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"])
    )
  }
) %>% mutate(direction = "MH -> Nea")

result <- rbind(result1, result2)

ggplot(result, aes(W, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ direction)
```
